row.title: FUTURE-AI: Guiding Principles and Consensus Recommendations for Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence in Future Medical Imaging
row.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "FUTURE-AI: Guiding Principles and Consensus Recommendations for Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence in Future Medical Imaging".
row.generation: Artificial intelligence (AI) has the potential to revolutionize medical imaging, but its adoption and implementation must be guided by principles that prioritize patient safety, privacy, and ethical considerations. This paper presents the FUTURE-AI initiative, which aims to establish guiding principles and consensus recommendations for trustworthy AI in future medical imaging. The initiative brings together experts from various disciplines, including radiology, computer science, ethics, and law, to develop a framework that addresses the technical, ethical, and legal challenges associated with AI in medical imaging. The resulting principles and recommendations cover areas such as data privacy, algorithm transparency, bias mitigation, and accountability. By adhering to these principles, stakeholders can ensure the responsible and ethical deployment of AI in medical imaging, ultimately benefiting patients and healthcare providers.

row.title: EdgeFlow: Achieving Practical Interactive Segmentation with Edge-Guided Flow
row.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "EdgeFlow: Achieving Practical Interactive Segmentation with Edge-Guided Flow".
row.generation: EdgeFlow is a novel approach to interactive image segmentation that combines edge detection and flow-based methods to achieve practical and efficient results. The proposed method utilizes an edge-guided flow algorithm to guide the segmentation process, allowing users to interactively refine the segmentation boundaries. The algorithm incorporates both local and global information to accurately capture object boundaries and handle complex image structures. Experimental results demonstrate that EdgeFlow outperforms existing interactive segmentation methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency, making it a promising tool for various applications such as image editing and object recognition.

row.title: EdgeFlow: Achieving Practical Interactive Segmentation with Edge-Guided Flow
row.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "EdgeFlow: Achieving Practical Interactive Segmentation with Edge-Guided Flow".

Traditional interactive segmentation methods often require user input in the form of markers or scribbles, which can be time-consuming and tedious. EdgeFlow addresses this issue by leveraging the inherent structure of edges in an image to guide the segmentation process. The proposed algorithm generates a flow field that incorporates both edge and color information, allowing for efficient and accurate segmentation. Experimental results demonstrate that EdgeFlow outperforms existing interactive segmentation methods in terms of both segmentation quality and computational efficiency, making it a practical solution for real-time applications.

row.title: Semi-supervised Contrastive Learning for Label-efficient Medical Image Segmentation
row.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "Semi-supervised Contrastive Learning for Label-efficient Medical Image Segmentation".
row.generation: Medical image segmentation plays a crucial role in various clinical applications. However, obtaining accurate and reliable segmentation labels for medical images is often challenging due to the high cost and time required for manual annotation. In this paper, we propose a semi-supervised contrastive learning approach for label-efficient medical image segmentation. Our method leverages both labeled and unlabeled data to learn a representation space where similar instances are brought closer and dissimilar instances are pushed apart. We introduce a novel contrastive loss function that encourages the model to learn discriminative features for segmentation. We evaluate our approach on two publicly available medical image segmentation datasets and demonstrate that it outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of segmentation accuracy while requiring fewer labeled samples. Our results suggest that semi-supervised contrastive learning can significantly improve the efficiency and effectiveness of medical image segmentation tasks.

row.title: Semi-supervised Contrastive Learning for Label-efficient Medical Image Segmentation

Our method leverages both labeled and unlabeled data to learn representations that capture the underlying structure and semantics of medical images. We integrate a contrastive loss function into the segmentation framework to encourage the model to pull together instances of the same class and push apart instances of different classes, using both labeled and unlabeled data. Experimental results on two medical image segmentation datasets demonstrate that our semi-supervised approach achieves superior performance compared to supervised methods that use only labeled data. Our approach significantly reduces the reliance on labeled data, making it a promising solution for label-efficient medical image segmentation.

row.title: Combo Loss: Handling Input and Output Imbalance in Multi-Organ Segmentation
row.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "Combo Loss: Handling Input and Output Imbalance in Multi-Organ Segmentation".
row.generation: Multi-organ segmentation is a challenging task in medical image analysis due to the imbalance between the number of organs and the amount of available training data. In this paper, we propose a novel loss function called Combo Loss to address the input and output imbalance in multi-organ segmentation. The Combo Loss combines the Dice loss and the Tversky loss, which are widely used in segmentation tasks, to achieve a balanced optimization between sensitivity and specificity. We evaluate the performance of the Combo Loss on two publicly available datasets and compare it with other state-of-the-art methods. The experimental results demonstrate that the Combo Loss outperforms existing methods in terms of segmentation accuracy and robustness. Furthermore, we conduct ablation studies to analyze the effectiveness of different components in the Combo Loss. Overall, our proposed Combo Loss provides a promising solution for handling input and output imbalance in multi-organ segmentation.

row.title: Combo Loss: Handling Input and Output Imbalance in Multi-Organ Segmentation

The Combo Loss combines two components: the Dice Loss, which evaluates the similarity between the predicted and ground truth segmentations, and the Focal Loss, which focuses on hard-to-segment regions. We conducted experiments on multiple organ segmentation datasets and compared the performance of Combo Loss with several state-of-the-art methods. The results demonstrate that the Combo Loss outperforms other approaches, especially in scenarios with significant input and output imbalance. Therefore, the proposed Combo Loss could potentially improve the accuracy and robustness of multi-organ segmentation algorithms in medical image analysis.

row.title: Segmenter: Transformer for Semantic Segmentation
row.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "Segmenter: Transformer for Semantic Segmentation".
row.generation: Semantic segmentation is a fundamental task in computer vision that involves assigning a class label to each pixel in an image. In recent years, deep learning models, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs), have achieved remarkable success in semantic segmentation. However, CNNs have limitations in capturing long-range dependencies and modeling global context. In this paper, we propose a new model called Segmenter, which is based on the Transformer architecture. The Transformer has shown great success in natural language processing tasks, but its application to computer vision tasks, especially semantic segmentation, is relatively unexplored. We adapt the Transformer to the semantic segmentation task by introducing a novel self-attention mechanism that operates on the spatial dimensions of the feature maps. Our experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that Segmenter outperforms state-of-the-art CNN-based models in terms of both accuracy and efficiency. Furthermore, we conduct ablation studies to analyze the impact of different components of Segmenter and provide insights into its working mechanism. Overall, our work highlights the potential of the Transformer architecture for semantic segmentation and opens up new avenues for research in this field.

row.title: Segmenter: Transformer for Semantic Segmentation
row.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "Segmenter: Transformer for Semantic Segmentation".
row.generation: Segmentation is a fundamental task in computer vision that involves classifying and delineating objects in an image. In recent years, deep learning approaches, particularly convolutional neural networks (CNNs), have achieved state-of-the-art performance in semantic segmentation. However, CNNs exhibit limitations in capturing long-range dependencies and context information, leading to suboptimal segmentation results. In this paper, we introduce Segmenter, a novel transformer-based architecture for semantic segmentation. We propose a hybrid approach that combines the strengths of CNNs and transformers, leveraging the localization capacity of CNNs and the contextual reasoning ability of transformers. Our architecture comprises a feature encoder based on a pre-trained CNN backbone and a transformer decoder that generates spatially correlated segmentation maps. We also introduce variational positional encodings and attention normalization to enhance the representation power of the transformer. We conduct extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, including PASCAL VOC and Cityscapes, to evaluate the performance of our model. The results demonstrate that the proposed Segmenter achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming existing CNN-based and transformer-based methods. Our findings highlight the effectiveness of combining the strengths of CNNs and transformers for semantic segmentation tasks.

We introduce a global contrastive loss that encourages the model to learn global features that are invariant to object appearance variations. Additionally, we propose a local contrastive loss that encourages the model to learn local features that capture fine-grained details of the objects. We evaluate our method on several benchmark datasets and demonstrate its superior performance compared to existing few-shot segmentation methods. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art results in terms of segmentation accuracy and generalization to unseen classes. Overall, our work contributes to the advancement of few-shot segmentation techniques and provides insights into the importance of global and local contrastive learning for this task.

row.title: Distribution-Free, Risk-Controlling Prediction Sets
row.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "Distribution-Free, Risk-Controlling Prediction Sets".
row.generation: This paper introduces a new method for constructing prediction sets that are both distribution-free and capable of controlling the risk of incorrect predictions. Traditional prediction sets often rely on assumptions about the underlying distribution of the data, which can limit their applicability in real-world scenarios. The proposed method, called Distribution-Free, Risk-Controlling Prediction Sets (DF-RCP), overcomes this limitation by leveraging the concept of conformal prediction. DF-RCP constructs prediction sets that are guaranteed to contain the true value with a specified probability, regardless of the underlying distribution. The method is demonstrated through extensive simulations and real-world examples, showing its effectiveness in various settings. The results highlight the advantages of DF-RCP over existing methods, making it a valuable tool for prediction tasks in diverse domains.

row.title: Distribution-Free, Risk-Controlling Prediction Sets
row.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "Distribution-Free, Risk-Controlling Prediction Sets".
row.generation: Prediction sets provide a framework for making probabilistic predictions in the form of intervals or regions rather than point estimates. Existing prediction set methods often rely on distributional assumptions and can be overly conservative. In this paper, we propose a distribution-free, risk-controlling method for constructing prediction sets that does not require any distributional assumptions. Our approach is based on minimizing the worst-case expected set size, which measures the average size of the prediction sets in the worst-case scenario. We derive a theoretical bound on the worst-case expected set size and develop an algorithm for constructing prediction sets that guarantees this bound. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on several real-world datasets and compare it to existing prediction set methods. Our results show that our distribution-free approach is able to provide accurate and calibrated prediction sets while avoiding the conservatism of existing methods.

Experimental results on various benchmark datasets demonstrate that our proposed approach achieves competitive segmentation performance compared to existing supervised and unsupervised methods. row.title: Double Similarity Distillation for Semantic Image Segmentation
row.prompt: Write the abstract for the academic paper titled "Double Similarity Distillation for Semantic Image Segmentation".
row.generation: Semantic image segmentation is a challenging task in computer vision that aims to assign a semantic label to each pixel in an image. Existing methods often rely on deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to learn discriminative features for accurate segmentation. However, these methods often suffer from high computational costs and limited generalization ability. In this paper, we propose a novel approach called Double Similarity Distillation (DSD) for semantic image segmentation. DSD leverages the concept of similarity distillation to transfer knowledge from a teacher network to a student network. Specifically, DSD consists of two stages: feature similarity distillation and spatial similarity distillation. In the feature similarity distillation stage, the teacher network and student network are trained to minimize the feature-level similarity loss. This encourages the student network to learn similar feature representations as the teacher network. In the spatial similarity distillation stage, the teacher network and student network are trained to minimize the spatial-level similarity loss. This encourages the student network to produce similar segmentation maps as the teacher network. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate that DSD achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of both accuracy and efficiency. Furthermore, ablation studies and visualization analysis are conducted to validate the effectiveness of the proposed method. Overall, DSD provides a promising solution for semantic image segmentation with improved performance and reduced computational costs.
